record.paper_title: Singularity Theorems in General Relativity: Achievements and Open Questions.
record.original_question: When a spacetime in general relativity is extensible and admits multiple inequivalent regular extensions, what physical criteria should be used to decide which extension is the physically appropriate one, especially when some candidate extensions remain singularity-free and others introduce singular behavior or violate conditions such as causality or energy positivity?

evidence.quote: which physical reasons are to be used to discriminate between inequivalent extensions?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Lorentzian spacetime satisfying the Einstein field equations, and suppose $(M,g)$ is extensible, i.e. there exists an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a proper open subset of a larger connected Lorentzian manifold $(\tilde M,\tilde g)$ (called an extension). Assume that $(M,g)$ admits at least two inequivalent regular extensions $(\tilde M_1,\tilde g_1)$ and $(\tilde M_2,\tilde g_2)$ (meaning there is no isometry between them that fixes $(M,g)$ pointwise), and suppose these extensions may differ in their global properties: for example, some may be geodesically complete or singularity-free while others contain curvature or incomplete-geodesic singularities; some may be globally hyperbolic and chronological while others contain closed timelike or causal curves; and some may satisfy standard energy conditions (weak, strong, dominant, or null energy condition) on the stress-energy tensor while others violate them.

Formulate a precise, principled set of physical and geometric criteria — and prove their consistency and applicability — that uniquely select, among all inequivalent regular extensions of an arbitrary extensible spacetime $(M,g)$, a preferred "physically appropriate" extension. In particular, the criteria should resolve cases such as the following: when one extension is singularity-free but violates causality or an energy condition, while another extension preserves causality and energy positivity but introduces singular behavior, which extension is to be regarded as physical, and on what grounds?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers (e.g., critical appraisals of the singularity theorems and work on low-regularity/holonomy extensions, 2021–2025) continue to discuss the non-uniqueness of spacetime extensions and emphasize that no universally accepted set of physical criteria exists to select among inequivalent regular extensions. The maximal analytic extension of Kerr is repeatedly cited as an example where the conventional choice violates causality, illustrating that the question remains conceptually open.

status_evidence.title: A critical appraisal of the singularity theorems
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses non-uniqueness of extensions and notes that the maximal analytic extension of Kerr leads to causality violation, leaving open which physical criterion should select an extension.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of choosing among inequivalent extensions is treated as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Spacetime Inextensibility Criteria by Volume-Distance-Ratio Asymptote
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes new geometric inextensibility criteria, indicating active ongoing research into when and how spacetimes should be extended.
status_evidence.claim: Selection criteria for extensions are still being formulated.

status_evidence.title: On holonomy singularities in general relativity & C^{0,1} extensions
status_evidence.snippet: Studies low-regularity extensions and shows non-uniqueness phenomena persist at low regularity.
status_evidence.claim: Non-uniqueness of extensions remains a live research issue.

status_evidence.title: Singularities and Black Holes (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews philosophical and physical debates about extensions and singular behavior, without endorsing a single criterion.
status_evidence.claim: There is no settled physical criterion for selecting extensions.
